I was asked yesterday for
certain explanations and certain reports. I was asked by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy)-

If the hon. minister will
allow me. the hon. member for Peace River asked me to let him know if the minister was going to bring down this information. He is engaged elsewhere at the moment, and perhaps the minister would give this information later.

Very well. There was also a letter written by the hon. member for Antigonish-Gusyborough (Mr. Duff) in connection with the Sarty's post office, and which was on my own personal file. I considered it personal and did not put it on the file that was brought down, but as it seems to be
the desire of the committee that the letter should be on the file, I am now tabling it.

We required only that
part of the letter which dealt with the post office.

Yes, and I now table it.
In connection with North Brookfield, it was claimed that a return tabled in 1928 was not complete, the only reference to the dismissal being a letter of instruction from the Postmaster General to the deputy. In this case also I am laying the complete file, including my own file, on the table.
In connection with the case brought up by the hon. member for New Westminster, I wish to read to the house my report on that ciase, and then to table the file. My report is as follows:
When Miss K. T. Mawson, the postmistress, requested that a male stenographer be appointed in her place, in response to her request for a statement of the duties of the position it was stated that stenographic work took up about one-half of the daily period, the other half being occupied in assisting the regular employees in the different departments where required. The Civil Service Commission reviewed the duties of the position and decided that it should be changed from postal clerk to stenographer grade 2, on account of the fact that his general duties were stenographic. The postmaster, however, represented that there were certain duties which he would not care to require a female to perform. Subsequent to Miss K. T. Mawson's resignation in July, 1928, Mr. Harold Wade was taken on and was appointed to the permanent staff as stenographer grade 2, as from January 29, 1926. In April, 1928, Mr. Wade was promoted to postal clerk, and the commissioners were requested to furnish the name of a male stenographer to replace him. They were unable to do so, and gave authority for a local selection. In consequence Mr. S. W. Thomas was employed temporarily from September 1, 1928. Subsequently the commission held a competition for stenographers at New Westminster, and on September 28, 1928, they submitted the name of Miss Margaret Isabella Moore, one of the successful candidates, in connection with the filling of the position permanently. In view of the postmaster's representations, however, the services of Mr. Thomas were retained and Miss Moore was not offered employment. It is understood that the Civil Service Commission advised Miss Moore, in reply to her inquiry, that the reason she had not been accepted by the department was that a male stenographer was necessary.
That is the explanation given to me by the officials of my department. It was purely a departmental matter and did not come before
Supply-Post Office

the minister at all. I am now laying the file on the table so the hon. gentleman can examine it.
Yesterday the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) asked for some information regarding Waterhole post office and Fairview post office. Here is the history of the case:
Waterhole is an old established office. It was opened on August 15, 1912. On January 29, 1928, Mr. David P. Smith, returned soldier, was appointed postmaster. Mr. Smith is still postmaster at Waterhole. Prior to Mr. Smith being appointed Mr. H. Sigler was acting postmaster. Mr. Sigler was applicant for the postmastership at Waterhole, and asked that if he were not successful in the appointment there he be considered as an applicant for the position of postmaster at Fairview.
Fairview post office. In 1920 authority was given for the opening of a new post office at Fairview, 44 miles from Waterhole. In submitting the application for the new office the district superintendent stated that there were two applicants, namely, Mr. Sigler and Mr. Levesque. In the first instance authority was given for the opening of the office at Fairview under the postmastership of Mr. Lesveque. In September the Postmaster General suspended action as he understood that Levesque was a non-resident. In November, 1928, the office was opened in charge of Mr. Sigler, who had been the former acting postmaster at Water-hole. Mr. Smith, the postmaster at Waterhole, inquired in regard to the possibility of his getting the appointment at Fairview, presumably on account of the increase in business at Waterhole, many of the residents having left for Fairview. Both offices are in operation at the present time. Mr. Smith is postmaster at Waterhole, and Mr. Sigler is the postmaster at Fairview. Up to the present time the postmaster at Fairview, Mr. Sigler, has been paid a salary of $100 a year. The postmaster at Waterhole, Mr. Smith, is still paid at the rate of approximately $1,000 a year.
The revenue of the Fairview post office from November 1, 1928, to the end of March, 1929, is $986. The revenue of the Waterhole office for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, is $1,423. The salaries will be adjusted on the above revenue bases at April 1, 1929.
Now, if the hon. gentleman wishes a copy-

I have a copy here. But my contention, Mr. Chairman, is that Smith was appointed to the Waterhole office by the Civil Service Commission. He is a returned soldier. All that exists at Waterhole to-day is the post office, a part of one of the three or four stores that were originally there, and a bunch of yawning cellars, the buildings having been moved to Fairview. The bank has also been transferred to Fairview. In a word, there is practically nothing left at Waterhole. The reason that Waterhole in the past was a rev-

enue office was due to the fact of its being the centre of the district so far as general business was concerned; but for the future the Waterhole post office cannot be anything else than merely a small country office for delivering mail. There is no question about that, because all business must go to Fairview, with its two banks, the only place where it can be transacted. In the very nature of things the Waterhole office must be attached to a store or given to someone who does not have to devote his full time to it. The civil service appointee is left there where he cannot make a living as postmaster under the natural order of things, as is well known to the post office superintendent of the district and to anyone else familiar with the circumstances. .
My contention is that when the town and the business was moved to Fairview, the appointed postmaster should have been moved there as well, with his office. It is purely a case of appointing a man through the minister -a political appointment, if you like-and leaving the other man, appointed by the Civil Service Commission, at Waterhole, in a job that is bound to run out as far as he is concerned.
He is left in the hole.

Yes, he will be in the hole all right. This office at Fairview has a peculiar record. I find on the file a letter from Mr. Levesque to the Postmaster General which reads as follows:
June 19, 1928.
In view of the fact that the Alberta government is extending the Central Canada railway fifteen miles west of the present terminus at Whitelaw to a townsite, which at present appears will be called Fairview, I wish to submit my name as desirous of obtaining the post office at the new town, whatever name is selected.
As the contract for the completion of the extension calls for early fall, I trust you can see your way clear to accept this as my application for the post office.
In support of this application I am taking the liberty of referring you to the Hon. Mr. Charles Stewart, Minister of the Interior.
Yours very truly,
J. D. Levesque.
On August 13 the district superintendent at Edmonton made two recommendations with regard to the appointment of a postmaster at Fairview. The first in order of merit was Henry Sigler, Fairview, the second J. D. Levesque, Peace River. He states in this report that the revenues of the office

at Waterhole will be affected adversely by the establishment of the new office. On August 25, 1928, we have this memorandum for the Deputy Postmaster General:
Re Fairview. Establish office and appoint Levesque.
In spite of the fact that he was second on the list. Now there is nothing to indicate what has happened, but I understand Mr. Levesque was a non-resident so far as Fair-view was concerned. There was a general and vigorous protest against this appointment by, I believe, the Canadian Legion, and as the minister has said, we have instructions issued by himself to suspend action. Very little was done for some months with regard
to the opening of the office, and while the town of Waterhole was being moved to the new site of Fairview a number of people who had become residents of Fairview and who
had previously been resident in Waterhole, wrote to the Postmaster General asking for the establishment of a post office. I wired the Postmaster General, and I think I made it perfectly clear that it was necessary to establish a new office; and it was also made clear that some change would be required with regard to the revenues of the post office at Waterhole. The following telegram was despatched, dated November 14, Fairview, Alberta, addressed to P. J. Veniot, Postmaster General, Ottawa, Ontario:
Waterhole village moved during last month five miles northeast to Fairview Alberta. New town end of steel, E.D. & B.C. railway. Fairview has six elevators, two banks six stores, no post office as yet. Post office should be established immediately.
(Sgd.) D. M. Kennedy.
Prior to this Mr. Smith, who was Postmaster at Waterhole, realizing what would happen when the town was being moved, wrote as follows:
Waterhole, Alberta,
September 24, 1928.
Postmastar General,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:
I wish to know if I could be transferred from Waterhole post office to the new post office at Fairview. If not, I wish to apply for the Fairview appointment. What salary would the postmaster at Fairview receive the first year? My reasons for the transfer are: There will be a school in Fairview, the nearest school to Waterhole is 1J miles distance, also the salary for the Waterhole appointment in the near future, I have heard, will be decreased.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) D. P. Smith,
Postmaster, Waterhole.
Supply-Post Office
On November 17 we have the following memorandum from the Postmaster General to the Deputy Postmaster General:
Re new post office at Fairview, Alberta Referring to memorandum September 8, you are hereby instructed to proceed immediately with the establishment of an office at Fairview. Mr. Henry Sigler, who is given first place m the district superintendent's report, of the 13th August, is to be placed in charge as postmaster.
This is rather a peculiar statement. Mr. Henry Sigler, it is said, is to be appointed postmaster because he is given first place by the district superintendent, but he was given first place before when Mr. Levesque was appointed. The report giving Mr. Sigler first place over Mr. Levesque was in the hands of the Postmaster General before he appointed Mr. Levesque. Then we have a wire to Mr. Leger, district superintendent of postal service, Edmonton, Alberta, under date of Ottawa, November 17, as follows:
Re Fairview. Take immediate steps to open office with Henry Sigler as postmaster.
(Sgd.) E. J. Underwood.
On November 21, 1928, Mr. Smith wrote to the Postmaster General as follows:
W'aterhole Post Office, Alberta.
November 21, 1928.
The Postmaster General.
Dear Sir:
In connection with the appointment for Fairview post office, I wish to know if Mr. Sigler has been appointed temporary postmaster, and if there is a chance of myself getting the appointment. If not, I would like to know how this office stands, will it be closed in the near future and salary decreased meantime.	[DOT]
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) D. P. Smith, P.M.,
Waterhole, Alberta.
On November 29, 1928, we have the following letter from E. J. Underwood to D. P. Smith, in reply to the letter I have just read: D. P. Smith, Esq.,
Postmaster,
Waterhole, Alberta.
Dear Sir:
In reply to your communication of the 27th November, regarding the opening of the post office at Fairview, permit me to inform you that there is no vacancy at that point as Mr. Henry Sigler was placed in charge as regular postmaster.
As regards the status of Waterhole, I may state that it will depend on the amount of patronage given it in the future. It is observed that it is over four miles from the townsite of Fairview and the question as to whether it will be maintained or not will depend on
Supply-Post Office

its revenue. The same applies to the salary attached to this office, which will be revised at the end of the present fiscal year and after the Fairview post office has been in operation for some months.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) E. J. Underwood,
Chief Superintendent of
Post Office Service.
And the-n we have some correspondence 'between the Postmaster General and Mr. Reilly, who is good enough to ask Mr. Smith whether he would resign his job at Waterhole in order that he might be transferred to Fairview-just about five hours before Reilly went to Fairview and appoint Mr. Sigler as postmaster there.
Now my point is that this returned soldier, who was appointed by the Civil Service Commission to the office in that district, should have been given the new office, which is and must be an important office, the others being merely subsidiaries. There was no misunderstanding so far as the department was concerned; it was understood in Ottawa as well as in Edmonton what was happening. In the first place Mr. Levesque was appointed on the recommendation of somebody whose letter is in the Postmaster General's file but is not produced in this file. Mr. Sigler had been recommended by the district superintendent at Edmonton first in order of merit and Mr. Levesque second, and after Mr. Levesque's appointment had to be cancelled Mr. Sigler months later was appointed on the direct recommendation' of the Postmaster General.
How can we expect a department the size of the Post office department to be efficiently administered and to be kept up to date if we are going to have the man at the head of the department taking charge of the details of appointments, political and otherwise, in the various small post offices throughout the Dominion? You might as well have Sir Henry Thornton going out west appointing section foremen. The Postmaster General has simply been playing politics in this instance, and anyone who is going to take up his time playing politics in this way cannot in my judgment pay proper attention to the big affairs in connection with his department. In addition to that we have a direct case of discrimination in actual fact against a returned soldier in favour of political appointees, and that is the reason why I speak on this occasion.

I cannot see how it is
possible that the hon. member (Mr. Kennedy) can say that there is any discrimination. In the first place, it was at an early date that the present postmaster at the first-named office, Waterhole, was appointed and accepted the position under the Civil Service Commission. For the same reason that I cancelled the appointment of Mr. Levesque at Fairview, because of his not being a resident, the Civil Service Commission would cancel the appointment of Mr. Smith to Fairview; because under the act no returned soldier nor anyone else can be considered who is not a resident of the place. That being the case-
Mr. Chairman

I did not interrupt the
hon. gentleman when he was speaking and surely he will accord me the courtesy of listening to what I have to say. There has been a little too much of this jumping up and interrupting the minister when he is endeavouring to make explanations. Surely the hon. gentleman who stands so firmly by the Civil Service Commission would not want me to undertake to violate the law; although no doubt he feels I should have done so in this case, surely he would not encourage me to do so. I had no option in the matter; there was only one thing to do and that was to appoint a postmaster to the position at Fairview, which was done. That is the only explanation I can give; there was no question of discrimination in my mind. The hon. gentleman has quite often referred to my discriminating against returned soldiers, and I feel the time has come when perhaps he might be told that my record with regard to returned soldiers from the beginning of the war to the present day is at least equal to if not better than his own.

I would like to correct
the Postmaster General; I did not make a general statement with regard to returned soldiers but I did make a statement with regard to this returned soldier.
We know what your intentions were, anyway.

I would like to
draw the attention of the minister-

Would my hon. friend
allow me to complete the returns I am to table? I was asked for a return having to do with the Waterford, Nova Scotia, post office, which I now submit to the house. I was also asked to complete the file in connection with the Conquerall Banks post office by

Supply-Post Office
adding certain letters which were on my own file. I am submitting herewith the additional letters; I think they are all from Mr. Duff and since he asked yesterday that they be submitted I have no hesitation in doing so.

Are all the files in the department dissected?
Mr. VENIOT; I do not think I need answer that remark. Now I wish to submit another return in connection with the Uffing-ton post office, and in doing so I wish to apologize to the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) because of certain figures I stated to the committee yesterday. This correction does not take away from the seriousness of the occurrences at that post office, but in revising the file which came from the finance branch of the department I find that instead of a shortage of $142 in 1926 the actual shortage was $24.43. However, that irregularity was continued later on and in 1928 a further irregularity was shown by an inspection on June 7, so with that explanation I am submitting the remainder of the file. Hon. members must remember that there are three different files in the department covering each of these matters, which may account for some of the files which have been submitted to the house not being complete. Then the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) requested information with regard to the postmastership at St. Davids, Ontario. When I left the department to come here that report was not ready, but they were working on it and if it comes in during the afternoon I will table it.

The minister promised
to bring a file for me, or to complete the file with reference to Sutton, Quebec.

When I left the office
they were bringing the correspondence up to date; I may have it this afternoon.

Would the minister state
whether or not a postmaster has been appointed at Sutton?

I could not say from
memory. I have something here with regard to St. Davids, which just came in, and which I will table. Mr. E. D. Lowry was suspended and resigned on November 18, 1927; a Civil Service Commission certificate was issued in favour of A. E. Woodruff; the certificate was accepted and he was placed in charge on March 1, 1928. As soon as the file with regard to Sutton comes in I will give it to the hon. gentleman.

Could the minister tell
me how many postal workers there are in Canada? I see the term used freely and I understand that it includes letter carriers in the cities. How many letter carriers are there and how many postal workers?
I will secure the information for my hon. friend.

I would like to
draw the attention of the Postmaster General to page 791 of Hansard for 1928, where the following question appears:
Dismissal of Postmasters
Mr. Brady:
1.	How many postmasters were dismissed throughout Canada from October 1, 1926, to February 1, 1928?
2.	During above period, how many of those postmasters were dismissed in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and
Prince Edward Island?
Mr. Veniot:
1.	421.
2.	British Columbia	 7
Alberta	 9
Saskatchewan	 34
Manitoba	 11
Ontario	 32
Quebec	 122
Nova Scotia	 106
New Brunswick	 99
Prince Edward Island	 1
Mr. Chairman, that is a period of exactly sixteen months, and not two years as the Postmaster General has stated. Upon figuring that out I find there is an average of twenty-six dismissals for each month; in other words, one postmaster was dismissed for every working day during a period of sixteen months. Apparently the Postmaster General thinks that the day is lost when he does not dismiss a postmaster. I would like the Postmaster General to furnish information as to how many of these dismissed postmasters were appointed by the Civil Service Commission.
I would like to refer to a question which I asked on March 18, 1929, as follows:
Post Office Department-Civil Service Recommendati ons
Mr. Stewart (Leeds):	_	_
What is the total number of cases in which the present Postmaster General, his deputy or his department, or either of them, have rejected or refused to accept the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission as to appointments?
Mr. Veniot:	32.
I would ask the Postmaster General to bring down the file referring to each of those
Supply-Post Office

thirty-two cases. We have only had two or three so far, and as this is a very important matter we would like to have, and I think we are entitled to have, all these files.
The Postmaster General has suggested that I am ignorant. I have endeavoured to obtain some information from the document from which he read and which he said was in the file, and upon which his remark was based. I asked the minister to table the document from which he was reading, and he did so. I now show7 that document to the house. The house can see that it is one sheet of foolscap paper filled in with long-hand writing, apparently copied 'by the Postmaster General or someone in his office. It simply contains a copy of Section 13 of the Civil Service Act, 191S, and what is said to be the ruling of the Department of Justice made on December 9th, 1919. I asked the minister yesterday if he would give the house the correspondence which resulted in the ruling referred to here. It is perfectly clear that it did not come from the Department of Justice in that form, and we would like to know from which department the request for this ruling came. If this information were furnished I could be enlightened on this ruling, and then he would not be able to reproach me in the future with being ignorant.
I told the hon. gentleman last evening that I would have the correspondence looked up, and I am endeavouring to find it.
It may come in two parts like the return I got.
I want the correspondence from the Department of Justice; the letter accompanying this ruling.
The Department of Justice will have to provide their own correspondence; I will provide anything that is in my department.
The minister gave the house to believe that he had the correspondence from the Department of Justice.

I did not do anything of the kind. I read the ruling of the Department of Justice as I found it, and which ruling I know js correct. I read it to the house and I was asked to put it on the table, which I did. I did not say that it was from the Department of Justice, I simply said that it was the ruling made by that department in 1919. I read the ruling and then a point of

order was raised that, having read from the paper, I should put it on the table. I placed the very paper I had in my hand upon the table of the house.
The Postmaster General left the impression that he was reading from the actual ruling of the Department of Justice.
No, no.
That is not fair.
The hon. minister says that is not fair, but will he dispute that that is not the ruling?
There is nothing to show that it is the ruling.

The hon. members know it is.
Mr. STEW7ART (Leeds): I do not know it, and I would like the information.

Will the Postmaster General
inform the committee at whose instance the ruling was made, and to whom the ruling was sent? If it was sent to his department one would imagine that it would be on one of the files. There is a little controversy over this matter and we should have it cleared up.

I said I would do that,
and I cannot do any more.
Does the Postmaster General know whether or not the ruling was asked for by his department? If he does not know that, then let the information be obtained.
I know the Civil Service Commission published their certificate stating the ruling of the Department of Justice.
I am not disputing that at all; that is not the issue before the committee.
I have promised to get the correspondence and will endeavour to find out how the ruling was asked for.
Can the minister say at the moment whether or not-
No, I cannot.

If the minister would permit me to finish he would have a better opportunity to answer it intelligently. Does the minister know whether his department asked for the ruling, and whether the ruling was addressed to his department?

It was made ia 1919.

Supply-Post Office
That is not an answer to my question. I do not oare whether it was made in 1919 or 1921; was it made at the request of the minister's department, and was the ruling given to his department?
I think it was, but I will find out and let the hon. gentleman know.
What we want is the. ruling itself.
It was made in 1919.
As it applies to all departments, what difference does it make?
I really believe the Civil Service Commission asked for it.
Is the hon. Postmaster General speaking to the house or is he just gossiping?

A little louder, please, so
I may be able to enjoy the laugh too.
I can tell whether the hon. minister is addressing the house by his standing up or sitting down.

The hon. member is a
good sportsman and I think he will agree that the Postmaster General has been more than generous in answering all sorts of interjections from hon. members opposite. They did not show him the courtesy of always rising in their places, and as a matter of good sportsmanship I feel the hon. member does not desire to convey the impression that the minister is mumbling his answers.

If my remark has annoyed the Postmaster General or the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), I shall have great pleasure in setting their minds at rest. I do not intend to hurt them any more than I can help.
During the debate yesterday the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Stinson), reviewed the series of remarkable events which had occurred in connection with the Picton post office. The Postmaster General attempted to reply to the remarks of the hon. member, and I would like to quote part of that reply which appears on page 1705 of Hansard. The minister said:
I am charged with refusing to appoint Mr. Way because, first, he was a soldier; it is said I should not have refused him.
The minister continued:
The second charge is that I should not have refused the certificate in his favour because of his experience as assistant postmaster. Let me point out that, according to the hon. gentleman's own statement. Mr. Way was assistant postmaster for twenty-three long years.
This is the argument that the Postmaster General advances against what was set up by the hon. member for Victoria:
Will the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Stinson) explain to the committee how it is that in 1912, when Mr. Petit was put out for
political interference, Mr. Way was not then promoted by the Conservative party. Why was he not recognized?
Mr. Stinson:	He was a much younger man.
Mr. Veniot: He had then been in the service seven years.
Of course the Postmaster General had not the facts in his mind when he referred to the matter, because Mr. Way at that time had been in the office for six years. He was a young fellow of twenty-two years of age, and he was not recommended, nor does the record show that he even applied for the position. As a matter of fact, he was advanced, as far as one could expect him to be advanced at that time, to the position of assistant postmaster at Picton.
But even supposing that was not the case,
I wish to draw the attention of the committee to one feature of the answer of the Postmaster General to charges of great importance that have been levelled against him in the house. His answer was to refer back ten, twelve, fifteen years to what some other party did when it was in power. Even, for the sake of argument, accepting his contention to its fullest extent, I ask hon. members: Does it put this government right that a preceding government did wrong? The Postmaster General's contention is that he is right in this case because a preceding government did the same thing. If a preceding government did something that was wrong, as I suppose most hon. members on the apposite side are prepared to accede to, then my hon. friend's contention gets him nowhere. His argument means only that the Postmaster General adopts revenge as his guiding motive in making appointments to postmasterships. As the cases that have been brought up have shown, the Postmaster General has been guided by one principle, and one only, not that of getting the best man for the position, not that of serving the public in the most efficient manner possible, but-and he glories in it

that to the victor belong the spoils and that the post office is fair game for patronage. That will have its reflection at some future date in the minds of the people of Canada. The Postmaster General smiles at that remark. The 'hon. member for Antigonish-Guvsborough very frankly admits that that

Supply-Post Office

is his proposal. Let me say that from this side of the house we have watched hon. members opposite during the discussion, and while the faces of many of them, as the details were brought out, showed the shame they felt at the position in which the Postmaster General had put them, still they apparently decided to applaud his action, and hon. members opposite must assume the full burden of acquiescing in and supporting these actions of the Postmaster General and the government.
The Postmaster General may smile, but I feel that this matter is one of very serious import. I shall be very much surprised1 if we do not find that the fire that has been lighted here to-day will blaze throughout the whole of Canada, not only in Conservative quarters but even in those normally supporting the government. My hon. friends may well take it to heart whether they should not join in some condemnation of the way in which this department has been managed, because they will hear about it when they go back to their constituencies. The people of Canada will not stand for manipulation, for political purposes, of the offices of this country in a service on which they depend day by day. I have some sympathy with the position of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough; he is frank; he says plainly: What are these offices for? Surely they are to be awarded to the people who support us. He can conceive of nothing else. That is his idea of politics, and he is frank enough to admit it. When I listen to the hon. member, the words of Byron come into my mind:
He was the mildest manner'd man
That ever scuttled ship or cut a throat.
For him I have a certain amount of grudging admiration because of his frankness, but not for members of the government who sit quietly in their places, because, unless they object actively and conscientiously, they must take some of the burden that the Postmaster General is loading on to the shoulders of the government and of his party at the present moment.
This file which I have in my hand narrates the story of the Picton post office. I shall go through it, not too tediously, I hope, but with sufficient thoroughness to impress certain points upon the minds of hon. members. Let me say in advance-and I think I can support my statement by what I shall show later- that the whole matter will develop simply and solely into a shameful plot to seek an opening with which to reward a partisan helper of the Liberal party. From beginning to end,

involved as it may be, it is simple to find the thread.	It had its inception in the
desire to reward a party worker, and it was carried through ruthlessly and without regard to any of the amenities of life in this country. It was carried through without sportsmanship, and I thank the Minister of Railways for that word. It was carried through in a way that reflects discredit on this government and on the country. I will ask the minister if he will give me a little help in regard to the file. I do so because the information in files we have received has not been complete and I think this one is in no less a state of incompleteness than some of the others. The file begins with four affidavits upon which presumably was founded the procedure, first, to oust the postmaster, and, second, to place a friend in the position thus made vacant. The affidavits are by Edward Sprague, Robert Purtelle, Hiram Ellis and Durward Cole. The first letter that we have is from the Postmaster General to his deputy, Mr. Gaboury, under date of April 1, enclosing four affidavits. Two or three of these deal with the political activities of the postmaster himself. It reads:
I desire to have an investigation held, first, into the political activities of this official.
That is the postmaster.
You can leave the charge of allowing gambling in the office for a later date.
I suppose if they could not get rid of him on the ground of partisanship, they would have a second string to their bow, and bring the man once more before a committee.
You will have the investigator call upon Mr. Robert Purtelle, John Edward Sprague and Durwiard Cole as witnesses and they will also provide further witnesses for the investigation.
It is quite plain, from reading that, that there was other correspondence. These four affidavits did not find their way into the possession of the Postmaster General without some correspondence, because in the affidavits there is no mention of the fact that these men headed by Mr. Purtelle would present further evidence. Therefore, on its face, the file, if it was a complete file originally, bears evidence of mutilation, and if it was not a complete file originally, it bears evidence of some negligence, almost criminal, in its preparation. I should be glad if the Postmaster General would take note of that, because I should like to see the letter Mr. Purtelle wrote. I judge it was he who came and saw the Postmaster General and put up the scheme to him, or who wrote a letter which the Postmaster General, according to his custom and practice, has put away in some personal

I heard Mr. Alexander McKee tell Mr. J. H. Roberts, Inspector of Postal Service, on December the 27th, 1926, that he (Mr. McKee) was in Picton post office on an election day and he (Mr. McKee) saw Samuel Smith, the postmaster instructing an elector' how and where to mark his ballot and directing him to the polling booth to register his vote.
Everyone in this house knows this much about the rules of evidence, that hearsay, to begin with is not supposed to be good evidence because you do not get direct to the man himself who is concerned, but hearsay of hearsay is pushing to an absurdity the taking of evidence and cannot be relied upon in any degree whatsoever. I want to compare what Purtelle swears to in that direct declaration with what was sworn to by McKee when face to face with the investigator. All he swore to in that investigation is that he resides at Picton and saw Mr. Smith during the campaign tell a man where to vote.
Why shouldn't he?

Certainly, it would be the duty of any decent man to help another man out. But Purtelle stretched that simple act to look like an incrimination of the postmaster telling an elector to vote Grit or Tory, or some other ticket, for I do not know what Mr. Raney was running for then.
There are two branches to the case, as I said. First of all, they had to get rid of Smith, who had been there for years. He had given offence to nobody, and was well thought of. There was no possible way of getting him unless "a plant" were framed. Purtelle wanted the job. He had worked for the Liberal party, and this was the reward he wanted to get. He found the Postmaster General perfectly agreeable to entering into the scheme with him, and this scheme was concoted by which affidavits would be forwarded and so sent on for an investigator to look at, and something might come of it. tleman in Sudbury, a political friend of the government, was told to go down to Picton and make an investigation. But he did not do so for months. He knew well what was expected of him. Finding it difficult through Mr. Purtelle's agency to get a place to hold the investigation, finally he suggested that he go down to Picton and go around to witness after witness and get evidence from them and call that an investigation; but Purtelle was wiser. I would not have thought that any man who has anything of the judicial in his make-up at all, who has anything in his make-up that inclines him to see fairness to the under-dog, would have bothered with the evidence for five minutes. I do not know whether the Postmaster General read the evidence and the finding or not. Mr. Plouffe had a great deal of trouble finding what was wanted, and that was some act of partisanship on the part of the postmaster. Everybody knew that that was what was wanted. The finding is simply this. Hiram Elis, one of the witnesses, said that he saw a man gambling for money with dice in the post office, but that was not the ground on which action was taken later, so I do not need to take up the time of the committee with that. Cole said that a certain room in the post office to which the mail couriers had access resembled a Tory committee room. He was a pretty solid Grit, and how he knew what a Tory committee room looked like I do not know, but he probably had some conversation with somebody in the mail sorting room in which the question of politics came u,p. It was an isolated case, as appears from the evidence. The postmaster said that he knew nothing o'f this. He had heard that there was some throwing of dice in the room, which he stopped, and he had heard nothing further about it, and believed that that was the end of it. Plouffe says that if the postmaster did not know all these things, he had at least con-

structive knowledge, as it was his duty as postmaster to exercise careful supervision. I would like hon. members to bear in mind that this finding is directed purely and solely against the postmaster. There was no indication that anyone else in the post office was concerned in the slightest way as having any responsibility for these things. Later on the importance of that will be apparent, but there is nothing in that biassed finding that indicates that any other official of the post office had any knowledge of the practices that were alleged to be going on.
A very amusing part, if you can find amusement in a tragedy, is the finding of this man Plouffe. But before I touch that, let me say that certain circulars came into the post office every day during the campaign, tied together in a bundle, with a label on, for rural free delivery. On that label were stamps affixed, and what the postmaster in that office did, and it was a very good practice, I suppose, was simply to hand the bundle to the courier on the route, and the courier delivered them to the boxes along the route or took them to another post office from where they would be delivered. All that was done in the Picton post office was to take these bundles of circulars, tied together and labelled and hand them to the courier. There was no, dispute about that at all. There was evidence that sometimes these circulars did not arrive when they should have arrived if posted at the hour certain men alleged they were posted. But how uncertain that is is shown by the affidavit of a man who said that he had posted them in the forenoon, and by the evidence of another man, who was a leader in that part of the conspiracy, who said he had posted them in the afternoon, and because these circulars did not get to the rural boxes next day before 3.30 the Picton postmaster is alleged to have held them up in the post office. Hon. members from the rural districts know well that these circulars may have passed through three or four different offices. In this particular case they passed through the Wellington post office, the Milford post office, the Picton post office, and then to the courier, and the Postmaster General must have known, if he had any desire to be fair, that if there was any delay-delay was not proven anyway-that delay might have occurred at the Wellington post office or at Milford or along the route. The evidence of the postmaster was that these circulars left his post office promptly on time. Plouffe says in his report:
The mail always came regularly to the box-holders, except during the electoral campaigns 
aforesaid. The majority of the witnesses making complaints were known to be active partisans for the Liberal side.
If the postmaster at Picton wanted to be dishonest, why would he hold up circulars going to Liberals who had always voted Liberal and would vote Liberal anyway? What harm or what good would it do for him to hold them up? Surely he would not be ass enough to do a thing like that. Now I read the reason for the finding of partisanship:
I infer from the evidence that the delay or non-receipt of the mail was caused by either one of the postmasters at Picton, Wellington or Milford, and I suspect that a great number of these irregularities originated at Picton.
Now, that is his finding. Mr. Chairman, you would not hang a dog on evidence like that. No man with the slightest sporting instinct or the least sense of fair play would deprive a man of his livelihood on evidence even ten times as strong as this flimsy finding. It is the flimsiest, slightest excuse for the exercise of political patronage that has ever come to my notice, and the Postmaster General should be thoroughly ashamed of himself and the government associated with him should repudiate the whole thing and reprimand the Postmaster General for his inexcusable action in the matter. It is incredible that this state of affairs should be allowed to continue in this country. Party politics? Of course. Political patronage? Of course. People believe in it to some extent. I saw my hon. friend from Yorkton (Mr. McP'hee) and my hon. friend from Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) and, I am sorry to say, my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Gray) applauding a statement made on this side that the Postmaster General thought it a day wasted when he did not fire a postmaster. That is their idea of "one good deed a day." They are the sort of boy scouts who are supporting the government.
I do not want to delay the committee longer than to say that to clear the way for appointing a friend this shameful deed was done and Smith, a postmaster of seventeen or eighteen years' standing, who had given entire satisfaction, was ruthlessly thrust out of the way. a minister who sets at naught the Civil Sfer-vice Commission and treats the Civil Service Act as though it were a mere piece of parchment, using his high office for the purpose of furthering political ends? When the estimates covering these salaries and allowances were before the committee last year the question of the salaries paid the lower grades of civil servants was discussed, particularly with reference to postal clerks, railway mail clerks, mail carriers and customs clerks, and during that discussion we found that many married men with families to support are included in the classes to which I have referred. In many cases these men are supposed to have an education more or less equivalent to high school entrance; we found that their examinations were such as to demand ability, a good intellect and physical health. The examination was both oral and written, in fact, these examinations included what are known as intelligence tests, and the work which these men are called upon to do requires hard labour, long hours and fidelity to the last degree. Anyone who has ever visited a post office employing nine or ten clerks will realize the amount of work entailed and the loyal service which is given. I wish to say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not know of a body of men more loyal and devoted to their work than the civil servants included in those classes which I have mentioned. When the heavy seasons come on twice a year, these men are continually on the job, and the extension of the commercial side of the Post Office Department has placed additional burdens upon them.
In spite of the fact that from all sides we are told that we have great prosperity

If we do not maintain in Canada a highly trained body of technical men engaged in research work we will be left far behind in the race for commercial supremacy. Therefore I trust that the commission will see to it that these technical men receive an adequate salary for the important work they perform.
In the past it was often thought that a university man was merely a theorist who loved to get away from the common walks of life, but I wish to say that the story of national research throughout the world redounds to the honour and the glory of university men of all countries. To-day we find men who have spent four years in college and perhaps another four years in post graduate work receiving salaries of about $3,300 annually. Is it the opinion of this committee that men possessing these high qualifications, men who are working hard and who, engrossed in their work, think nothing of time, are well paid by a salary of that kind? I say that is not so.

I would like to mention the fixing of a minimum at $100 per month. Can $1,200 per year be considered as anything else but a minimum wage for mail carriers, postal clerks, and three or four other grades? A great number included in these classes are receiving only $75 to $90 per month. A great number never reach the maximum of $1,500 per year. It takes seven or eight years to reach that maximum, and many of them find that they have to go out and obtain seasonal employment which will bring them a larger return. Is that being fair to this very deserving body of civil servants?
Another thing which interested me during the course of the debate of the last few days was the sad story which brought to our attention of what was called malversation. I think
it speaks well of the probity of this great class of workers that so little pilfering or stealing has taken place. I do not know of any body which is entitled to as much respect for their honour and integrity as are these men who are engaged in such important work, and on such meagre pay. I think no apology should be offered, nor is any apology needed, for any member of parliament to advocate that these civil servants should receive due consideration and that the matter of adjustment of their salaries should be taken up immediately'. The public at large are watching very interestedly the proceedings of the Civil Service Commission. The salaries of the deputy ministers are to be increased and I wish to show the house that their salaries have risen very high in the last ten years. In fact, I find that in the last-ten years the salaries of deputy ministers have increased by 100 per cent. There may have been a very good reason why the deputies should have their increases first and I trust this is the right one. The government may feel that, by increasing the salaries of the deputy ministers first, it may be better able to increase the salaries of the technical and professional men and then bring up the question of the salaries of the lower classes, so that the gulf may not be too wide which separates them from the top. The people of Canada appreciate the fact that the civil service of all grades are entitled to a living wage. In the last session of parliament the arguments advanced why reclassification and adjustment could not take place were, to my mind, nothing more than " passing the buck," if I may use that term. No sound arguments were given why this problem should not be taken in hand. If the Postmaster General and the Civil Service Commission were in earnest, progress could certainly be made. Are we to have another year pass by without a readjustment being made in regard to the lower grades? I hope not.
Coming back to the position in which we are to-day, I believe that the honour of parliament is at stake. At this very moment throughout the length and breadth of Canada we are being told that the high offices which should be sacred under all conditions, have been used for lower motives than that of the public interest. It is a pitiable travesty upon the intelligence of the people of Canada to have it said in- this house that because in the past things were done that were derogatory to good government, they should likewise be done to-day. That is not my view. I think the public of Canada will not take that view, but they will demand purity and integrity in every department that appertains to the
Supply-Post Office

well-being and interest of the people. Why should the Civil Service Act be set aside? When people sit for an examination and pay to get it; when they receive their marks for it, they believe that merit alone will decide. That apparently is not the case. Why should men have to travel hundreds of miles, as I have known them .to do, to sit for some examination and then find that, though they passed first, either they did not get the position or it was months and months afterwards before they were able to get the jobs for which they passed? Is that the case in other countries ? I do not think so. We stand for legislative purity. If there is a Civil Service commission whose duty it is to hold examinations in various parts of Canada, and if they are carrying that out rightly, there should be no danger that the right man does not secure the position. Whatever may happen in this house; whatever explanations the government may later offer; whether or not they may accuse this side of the house of using a dramatic episode to further their own interest, that will not avail, 'because the gravity of the situation is such that the people of Canada, realizing the importance of justice being done, will speedily come to the conclusion that the time has arrived when a full investigation should be made into the relationship that exists between the department of the Postmaster General and the Civil Service Commission. The question is this: Who is responsible? Is there a liaison between one and the other? Are they acting independently, or is one subordinate to the other? This is a very important matter which parliament should understand, and I trust, before this item passes, the government will decide upon a definite policy and let parliament and the people of Canada know what it is.

Many years ago, I, like
many others in the Dominion of Canada, was appointed ipostmaster at the splendid sum of $10 per annum. That was under the government of Sir John A. Macdonald. I cannot understand what the hon. member who has just closed his remarks means about university men. after four years .preparation and an additional post graduate course of four years, being able to get a salary of only 83,000 a year. I have known many young men in the past fifty years, especially in the last ten or fifteen years, who have taken technical courses of two years-naturally they were adapted to the course or they would not have taken it-and who are being paid salaries of many times S3,000. I cannot understand why we need university men who have also under-
taken post graduate work, spending eight or ten years in getting an education, for the position of rural mail driver or country .postmaster. It seems strange to me. I would think that their fathers and mothers would become martyrs in furnishing the money that would be required for so much worthless education for a position of that sort.
Why worthless?

I have had ten years of Sundays in my life, and we have all spent a few years in infancy and childhood, and then we sleep one-third of our time, and if out of the time that is left we are going to spend eight or ten years in getting an education at a university simply to become a rural mail driver or a country postmaster at the end of it all, I cannot see that it is worth it. I think people have got to come down nearer to earth. The earth gives us all we need if we use it well. We have to scratch mother earth to earn our daily bread.
Let me give my own experience as a postmaster. After being postmaster for thirty-six years I voted for reciprocity, and I was driven out of office. In my opinion too many post offices have been closed up in this country and too many rural mail routes established. My particular office was at the outlet of a lake, in quite a business centre, with two churches, a school, and a Catholic mission. I have one of the biggest stores in the country and sell all sorts of merchandise. I would not say for one .minute that a young man should spend eight years at a university and do post graduate work before I could recommend him to the Postmaster General, and have the post office at Baldwin's Mills reopened. I should want a young man who was honest and intelligent. I was willing to accept the office in the old days at ten dollars a year.
I was a grist miller by trade, and I was intending to build a store, and I built it and filled it. I think that a post office in a country store attracts customers. I do not see why a person of ordinary intelligence could not entertain the customers without having to spend four years at a university and four years in post graduate work, nor do I think that eight yearss' university training is necessary to become a rural mail driver. It is true that a postmastership is a sacred trust.

Will the hon. member permit
a question?

You make too many
speeches and talk altogether too much. I waste very little of the time of the house

myself. I remember the first time I ran for parliament. I ran against a very brilliant man, and I promised my constituents that I would not waste the time of this house by speaking whenever the opportunity occurred, but only when duty demanded. But I am on my feet now, and I propose to explain a few matters.
I was saying that the office of postmaster is a most sacred trust. When I was put in charge of a post office, the arrangement was to furnish the postmaster with a certain quantity of stamps, and when he ran short, he would order more. I think it was a splendid arrangement. Thirty years ago the postmasters were allowed to keep on hand stamps up to fifty, seventy-five, a hundred or a thousand dollars' worth, depending upon the size of the post office, and the postmaster was charged with those stamps. I think every hon. member knows that when a postmaster runs short of stamps he must send the necessary money to Montreal or Ottawa or to the chief post office in his district to get a further supply, and send cash with order. How this man could be short, I do not understand. I always mix my business right together. I have no time to take inventories, keep cash accounts; I work fifteen hours a day. Anybody in my employ does not have to steal from me, and if the inspector had called at my office he would 'have found fifty dollars' worth of stamps somewhere around my establishment. I would not be short, but some of these kitchen post offices may have been short, I suppose. It is a very sacred trust, but I think any honest and intelligent person is qualified to fill the office.
The hon. member who preceded me delivered an oration, rather than saying something that applied to the practical things of life. I know, of course, that an education is good for a young man, if he has lived long enough to know what he is adapted to; he can then qualify for the vocation or profession he intends to follow, but why the hon. member delivered an oration on university and post graduate education in connection with rural mail couriers and country postmasters, I cannot understand. To get such an education you may use all your money and get into debt, and then it might be natural for you to steal if you got the chance. I do not want to mention it, but it is an absolute fact that it has been rather too common in this great Dominion for men in the larger post offices to steal. If a postmaster was allowed two or three thousand dollars' worth of stamps, he would sometimes live beyond his means, and by-and-by report a burglary. The inspector
goes there and finds that not a nail has been pulled, not a screw removed, not a panel broken. In fact, some of these postmasters were so derelict in their duty that they did not lock the vault. Some of them would accuse the night watchman and say that he had robbed the mail. I have known men to 'try to get the night watchman imprisoned, but when I had something to say about it,
I would get Mr. Coolican at Ottawa to send out a real detective, without fear or favour for anyone, one that did not care for Liberals or Tories, and get him to make a thorough investigation. Perhaps the postmaster was a man of considerable influence, and could fool the auditors that were brought in, for figures can be fooled, but figures will not lie. I would tell the detective to work on the theory that the man was guilty, and to get. the money back, and the accused has sometimes broken down and said to the detective. "You have come here to arrest me?" "Yes." "Would it be an extenuating circumstance if I reimbursed the government?" "It certainly would," says the detective. "Then I will try." The detective goes back. He says, "Now, Mr. Gentleman, I want you to tell me when you commenced this theft. Write it all out." When the confession has been made the detective says:	"Now, you
resign from this office." The man says, "All right, but I don't want to resign." The detective retorts, "It is not for you to say. Hand your keys right over and get out." The fellow says, "But I want my hat and coat." "Get out!" says the detective, "I will throw them out to you."
But coming back to my oratorical friend who preceded me, I cannot see the necessity for a man of university training to act as a country postmaster or a mail carrier either in our urban centres or rural districts. It is so amusing to me that it prompted me to get on my feet, and, Mr. Chairman, having expressed my views thereon I will not encroach further on the time of the committee.

I want to refer again

Whether he intends to or not-and I am rather inclined to be generous enough to think that he does-that man's reputation has been tarnished. I have here the further returns which the minister was good enough to bring down today, and I find that on one occasion last summer when the inspector walked into the postmaster's office he found this man short eleven dollars and some cents; that amount should have been in the till and was not there. I appeal to any member of this house: How many men who are handling public funds can have an inspector walk in on them any hour of the day, not knowing that he is coming, and always have every last cent in the till? I ask any reasonable man this question: If there are a few dollars missing at the moment, not in the proper place, when an inspection is made, is that any indication of dishonesty? He is an old man, is unable to walk, and has not a cent in the world.

That has not yet been

General to make a statement to the effect that there has been no dishonesty on the part of this man, because I do not believe that the Postmaster General is of that opinion.

Referring once more to the matter, I think that if the hon. member will read what I said yesterday he will find that it does not convey the impression that I thought this gentleman really dishonest, because I said there were irregularities that could not be classed as dishonesty.

But in cases where attention is frequently called to these irregularities and no heed is paid by the parties to whom such attention is directed, it becomes a matter for action. In this case, when the first irregularity took place-and I regret, as I have said before, that last night in the heat of debate I could not put my hand on the precise figures when I mentioned the sum of $142, because I have no intention to represent it as greater than it was-this postmaster was severely reprimanded and was told that if such a thing occurred again severe action would be taken. But notwithstanding that, m June, 1928-I believe it was around that date, because it was some time around October or December, 1926, that he was reprimanded, although I am not sure of the dates -the report of the inspector shows that there was a similar occurrence. Now I do not wish to hurt anyone's character; far be it from me; and if my remarks left the impression that it was because of dishonesty I wish to say that it was because of these irregularities in his accounts. I do not believe that the gentleman is fitted for the office, because of his age, and in addition there were these irregularities. That is what I believed at the time and what I believe now.

I am glad to have that much from the minister. I am within the judgment of the house when I say that he was not quite so moderate yesterday, and even to-day he has overstated the case. I have in my hand the latest file which the minister was good enough to give us, and there arc really only two cases, one several years ago involving $24 and one in 1928 in which the amount, as the Postmaster General says, was $7 or, according to the inspector, $11 odd. I submit in all seriousness that when a man is handling public funds as a postmaster in a store, or in any other place you like, if an 
inspector walks in upon him at any moment and happens to find a few dollars not in the till, that is not a very serious reflection on the man. I have mailed a copy of that letter to the Postmaster General's department and I want to impress upon him the need for this service.
We will go right into it the moment I receive that copy. I do not know of any official report as to this condition, but we will go into the matter as soon as I receive a copy of that letter.

I want an investigation into the Victoria post office; for the last two or three years the business of the office has so increased that the men have been overworked. I want it distinctly understood that there is no question as to the fidelity and earnestness of the whole staff from the postmaster down, but we do claim that too much work has been put upon them, particularly since the government have not seen fit to arrange for any increase in salary. The technical men are being looked after, but the mail men who walk the streets of our cities cannot get an increase. In my own district of Victoria when the mail bag is full they must pick up two or three bundles of papers which they relay, leaving them on a veranda or in a hodse and going back for them after they have delivered some of their other mail. I am sure
two or three additional men would relieve that situation; some better system could be put into effect in Victoria without a great deal of trouble. Is it right that a city whose post office revenue increased more than $24,000 in one year should have an increase of only $340 in the estimates? I ask the Postmaster General to go into that question also. .
The technical men practically have had their increase granted; perhaps they are entitled to it. I like to see everyone well paid, but if the Postmaster General would see that the salaries of these men were increased he would be doing a great service. I would like him to correct me if this statement is wrong:	I
understand that the men who walk the street carrying mail from house to house have no chance to get into the inside service. Is that so?

No, that is not so; they
can be promoted.

I just asked that question for my own information, because I did not want to be misinformed. The outside men must endure the vicissitudes of the weather, and most of them are broken in health; that must be the case even more in the east than in the city from which I come, but at all events I think the department should take that into consideration and advance the salaries of these lower salaried men.
Then I want to ask if it is to be the policy of the government in the future to appoint a commission whenever a branch of the service requests an increase. That is the precedent which has been set by this government, and in future any branch of the service asking for an increase no doubt will ask the government to appoint a similar commission.
Now let us see if the government is playing fair. I notice in the estimates an item of $800,000 increase for air mail services. Is it not a fact that, at best, for some years to come the air mail service will be uncertain or just an experiment? Does it seem fair to the post office employees that this amount should be placed in the estimates for such a service when the regular service employees cannot secure a slight increase? I would not care so much about the increase if they were not worked to death. In conclusion I ask the Postmaster General to look into these matters and do justice to Victoria. I could bring him half a dozen letters similar to the one I read a few minutes ago. I promised my constituents that I would bring up this matter in the house and I believe we are entitled to more consideration.

I wish to offer a few observations with regard to what I consider a glaring flouting of the Civil Service Act; I refer to the post office at Billings Bridge. That post office became vacant early in December, 1927, as a result of the improper conduct of the postmaster, a man named Dowler. There was a shortage of funds and after an investigation it was proved beyond doubt that Dowler was responsible and he was dismissed, which was the proper thing to do. The Deputy Postmaster General got in touch by letter with the hon. member for the county of Russell (Mr. Goulet) pointing out the reason for the change and asking the member to nominate some reliable person who could be temporarily placed in charge of that office. The shortage in the accounts was in connection with the issuing of money orders and the Deputy Postmaster General asked that the temporary appointee should be a person who could be trusted to issue money orders. He also stated that steps would be taken to fill the position permanently in. accordance with the provisions of the Civil Service Act. The member for Russell replied on November 30, 1927, to a letter from the Deputy Postmaster General dated November 22, 1927. The hon. member nominated a prominent business man of the village named Campbell, and that gentleman was appointed. Ordinarily one would ask why the Civil Service Commission was not notified and asked to take immediate steps to fill the position permanently. Campbell continued in this temporary position and we find that the Assistant Deputy Postmaster General, whose apparent duty was to notify the Civil Service Commission as to this vacancy, did not notify the commission until March 19, 1928. The following letter was written on that date by Mr. Coolican, Assistant Deputy Postmaster General, to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission:
I beg to inform you that the postmastership at Billings Bridge, electoral district of Russell, Ontario, is vacant owing to the dismissal of Mr. George M. Dowler, O.A.S., in connection with shortage in his accounts.
You will find herewith copies of poster notices issued by the district superintendent of postal service at Ottawa.
Poster notices in French and English were enclosed with the letter. The notice reads:
Applications are invited from residents of Billings Bridge and locality possessing the necessary qualifications for the position of postmaster at Billings Bridge.
Salary and allowances $1,000, based upon the revenue of the post office; rent allowance $150;

forward allowance, $9; allowance of one cent on each postal note issued (in the event of money order business being reestablished, allowance of four cents on each money order issued and one cent on ea :h money order paid).
Qualifications required: ability and education to efficiently perform the duties of office.
The notice stated that the applications should be received by the district superintendent of postal service, Ottawa, not later than March 27, 1928. That notice was sent to the Civil Service Commission on March 19, 1928, and the applications were to be received not later than March 27, eight days later.
There may be some reason for this delay, but I do not think it is a clear one in this case. I looked for an explanation in the correspondence which took place between the Deputy Postmaster General and the member for the riding, and I found a letter from the Deputy Postmaster General to the hon. member, but it is in French and I cannot read it.
That is too bad.

That is too bad, but I will give the house the substance of it. The Deputy Postmaster General, in the correspondence to which I have referred, informed the hon. member of the vacancy and the necessity of filling it, having regard to the public inconvenience occasioned thereby. He said it was necessary that a permanent appointment be made at once; that it would be necessary to make a new appointment and replace Mr. Dowler. The hon. member for Russell replied to that letter, and on December 16, the assistant deputy minister wrote him a letter apprising him of the temporary apointment of Campbell. The hon. member wrote to the Deputy Postmaster General on December 20, asking that the matter be allowed to stand until they could have a conversation with reference to it. The Deputy Postmaster General replied to that letter on December 22, stating that the matter would be held up until they could discuss it. In other words, the delay from December to March was due to the desire of the officials of the departments to confer with the local member regarding this matter, a matter which under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, should have been attended to immediately. The position should have been advertised and applications received by the district superintendent, which applications should have been reported upon to the Civil Service Commission so that the matter could have been dealt with. But that was not done.

Royal College of Physicians
The time expired on March 27, and within that period applications were received from J. L. Brule, a resident civilian; D. T. Campbell, a resident civilian-the temporary appointee; John Sinclair, a resident civilian; and C. W. Cummings, a non-resident civilian. It seems to me that the district superintendent could have proceeded and made his report, and we find that he did make a very extensive report which covers three pages of this return. This is return No. 185, dated March 9, 1929, made on the motion of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) acting for the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart). In this report Mr. Low, district superintendent, refers to the four applicants. He gives the detailed answers in respect to the oral examination and the written examination made by each of these men, Brule, Campbell, Sinclair and Cummings, and he also makes lengthy comments. But that report was not sent to the Civil Service Commission. I do not understand why it should not have been sent on, because the very object of getting a report is to advise the Civil Service Commission. It was, however, not sent to them.
On April 2, the district superintendent received an application from another man, Phillips. That was in his hands just about the time he made this report. That was not sent on, but the department took time to make an investigation of the application. I find from the file that the district superintendent makes tiwo lengthy reports in regard to Phillips, although the application was received on April 2, which was too late. Phillips was a returned soldier, a man who had not been wounded, and who had no disability. He had served overseas, and he had lived in the district for some time. April 16 is the date of the district superintendent's first report in which he reported favourably in regard to this man. On April 19 the chief superintendent of the postal service writes back to the district superintendent, asking him to state where Mr. Phillips' name should appear in the order of merit of the applicants. In other words, although the time had gone by within which applications might be received, the officers of the department were quite willing to consider this application and ask where it should be placed in the order of merit.

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext: Perhaps I had better give a short explanation to the house. This bill is asked for by the Canadian Medical Association, which, as its name implies, includes in its membership medical men from every province in Canada. This has nothing whatever to do with education; it has nothing to do with the licensing of medical men. The Canada Medical Act has to do with the licensing of medical men in the provinces. The whole object of this bill is to encourage post graduate education. When a man has been graduated for three years and is licensed to practise medicine in one of the provinces of Canada, he is eligible to be admitted to fellowship in this organization. The idea is to encourage post graduate education, the fellowship being a recognition that the post graduate studies have been taken. This body has nothing to do with education.

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext: There is a marked distinction between this bill and what is called the Roddick bill, under which the medical council has to arrange for examinations and award some recognition to anyone passing their examination. That was and still is subject to the approval of each province. At the present time any province can separate itself from the Dominion council1. As the hon. member for Saskatoon says, the purpose of this bill is to encourage a higher standard of education. Anyone who wishes to submit himself for examination may do so; it is entirely a voluntary matter. It is not in connection with qualifications for practice. It is somewhat similar to the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons in London, in Edinburgh and in Dublin. It is intended as an incentive to medical men, both physicians and surgeons, to aspire to higher qualifications and, therefore, higher standards.

Royal College of Physicians

speechtext:

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext: My hon. friend says that this has nothing to do with education, and of course I take his word for it. maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext:
We are simply
adopting the same title as that of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons in London, in Edinburgh and in Dublin. It is really not intended to have any control of education, nor, as I said before, has it anything to do with the licensing of medical men. It is simply an organization of medical men formed to promote a higher standard of professional education in the Dominion. It will be observed that every medical man must be a graduate of three year's standing of a medical school or university and must also be licensed to practise medicine in one of the provinces of Canada before he is permitted to take the examination. Having passed the examination and become a member, he in effect tells the world that he has taken this post graduate course. The idea is to encourage a larger number of medical men to continue their studies in the interests of the general health of this country.

But more recently there was formed in the United States an American college of surgeons. I may be wrong, but while we say this proposed royal college is modelled on the British institutions to which I have referred, really its purpose is to put us on a par with the American college.
