maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext:
I want to join with the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Man-ion) in advocating the passage of this bill. I think it is time that Canadians had an institution of this kind of their own. In the past we have been too prone to pride ourselves upon the degrees we have won in colleges either within the British Empire or in some of the American states, and I hope the time has come when Canadian academicians will stand on their own feet. Surveying the field of industrial and scientific research, I think we may safely say that no universities in the world to-day, of all those that loom up on the intellectual horizon, are greater tjian the universities of Canada. There is no country in the world where the medical profession has attained greater achievements than in Canada. This legislation therefore is only, so to speak, to put the final seal of accomplishment and of recognition upon the profession. It is no secret in the medical profession that every member of that profession prizes most the degree obtained from the Royal College of Surgeons of London. It is true we get degrees from Edinburgh and Ireland as well. But speaking as one whose pleasure and honour it has been to have graduated from the Royal College of Surgeons in England, I recognize this as one of the greatest achievements of my life; I believe it is recognized in academic and medical circles
rMr. Lapointe.]
as one of the most coverted honours to have graduated from that college. I am not prepared, however, to admit that we in this country should not establish an institution of our own, whose degrees it will be equally the ambition of every Canadian to secure. I have much pleasure in supporting the bill; it is, I think, a measure which is long overdue. We Canadians 'have too great a tendency to hide our light under a bushel. We are not good1 enough advertisers; we do not make the accomplishments of our people known to the world in the way we should. All we need do is to scan the achievements of our universities and to take the standing of our professors, and I say without fear of contradiction that the Canadian is the peer of any not only in the British Empire but in the world. I join with others who have spoken in urging the favourable consideration of this bill, for I know that this legislation will be of benefit to scientific education in Canada.

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext:
I do not desire
to delay the passage of the bill, but as a medical man and a graduate of a Canadian medical school I feel I ought at least to say a word in support of it. As my hon. friend across the way (Mr. McGibbon) has observed, Canadian medical institutions are outstanding not only on this continent but throughout the world, as institutions that give a broad medical education. This is proved by the fact that Canadian graduates 'have been able to go to various countries where medical science has attained a high standard and there compete with those who have had the best training in the world's universities. The bill does not affect in any way the institutions now engaged in the education of medical men in Canada, but it will give to Canadian graduates or graduates from other universities an opportunity to secure what I am sure will be a coveted degree in the profession of which I am glad to have been and to be now a member. 1 thoroughly endorse the bill and the proposal it contains. Our medical profession has so advanced in Canada, and has attained such a standing in the medical world, that I believe we can now very well proceed to found an institution to be known as the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada.

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext:
I took part in the debate
in this house at the time the Canadian Medical Association was created, and the conclusion arrived at then was that that legislation could not become effective until the various provinces had endorsed it. In con-

Premier Guarantee Insurance Company
nection with that legislation, the question arose whether a university in Quebec or in Ontario could grant a diploma which would be recognized in any other province.

speechtext: I understand that this bill does not touch that question at all. I believe that the Canadian Medical Association has since granted diplomas enabling medical men to practise in any part of the Dominion. I understand that that is the system.

speechtext: Without examination.

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext: That does not affect in any way the powers held at present in the provinces. The only other point to which I wish to draw attention is the use of the word " royal." I think it would be wise to not pass the title until the Secretary of State can communicate with the imperial authorities with regard to the use of that word. This question has been discussed in this house several times, and each time this communication from the British government was requested.

maintopic: ROYAL COLLEGE OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS OF CANADA
speechtext:
In that regard I took the trouble to communicate with the Solicitor General, and his opinion is as follows:
In reply to your letter of the 15th instant regarding the use of the word "royal", I may say that the usual practice is to obtain the consent of His Majesty to the use of the word. I observe, however, that in the ease you have in mind the intention is to have the name including the word "royal" conferred by act of the Dominion parliament, and, while you will appreciate that it is not my function to a druse you, I think the passage of such a bill, to which His Majesty is a party, would render it unnecesary to apply to His Majesty for consent.

I am quite sure that many members of the house had never realized that this was not ordinary private legislation which was going through; that we were acting as a court of justice, and, therefore, that we should take all precautions in law and equity which any court of justice has to take. With the volume of this work growing from year to
year it is intellectually and physically impossible for the committee charged with the examination of these cases to carry on with their work, and I do not say that in any spirit of disparagement of the committee of the senate or the private bills committee. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out last week, it has been necessary at times to look through the halls and corridors in order to find a quorum for the private bills committee to vote upon a batch of twenty or thirty of these bills. No tribunal would ever attempt to deal in such a manner with twenty or thirty cases of law; the most trivial cases are always considered on their merits. Is the annulment of a marriage a less important thing than the most trivial cases that come before police courts or criminal courts or civil tribunals every day? We have let the system grow without realizing the seriousness of our responsibilities. I say in all earnestness it is not a matter of pleasure for me, any more than it has been for any other member who has taken the same position, to delay the business of the house. I would not feel insulted' at all if anybody accused me of blocking this legislation in order to give the house time to reflect over it. I am doing this in a sincere desire to do something good for my country. I think the government should examine the situation and come to some decision with regard to all these bills and the principle and basis of them. It is for the purpose of emphasizing upon the minds of the members of the government, the members of the house and the people generally, the seriousness of the situation that has grown upon us, that I for my part have taken this view, and I think it was also the view taken by other hon. members who have approached the question from another angle.

Supposing the charges dealing
with practically the only ground upon which divorce is granted were proved to the hilt in the senate committee, would my hon. friend still oppose the bill?
Yes.

I have not read the evidence in this case, but I have in a number of them and in every single one in which I have read the .evidence, the charges have been proved to the hilt. If my hon. friend says that it is not on the question of proof he is opposed to the bill, he would simply vote against it no matter what the evidence was, and he would still let people come to parliament, this being the only course they can take in Ontario, and spend $500 to $1,000 and yet, although
Procedure Respecting Divorce

they conform with the law, produce the evidence which is reported and presented to the house-and my hon. friend has a copy of it in his room; as far as I know every hon. member gets it-he will deny to those people a right which is held out to them as citizens of Canada. Surely that is unfair.

What I have been trying to emphasize in these various debates, not only this year but last year, is the necessity of amending the constitution and, short of that, of amending the procedure. In years past the question has been discussed only academically; nothing has been done. The same procedure has been going on from year to year and the senate is complaining about it.

So far as I know, the only
complaint the senate make is that they want a different forum; they want a judge, who is trained to this sort of thing, to do it, and not have the time of the senate and of this house wasted as it is from year to year.

Quite so, but at the
same time that raises the bigger issue which I am not going to discuss to-night, because some other occasion will be found to discuss it-that is, the question of provincial as well as federal jurisdiction.

Which does the hon.
member stand for?

Unhesitatingly for the
exclusive and absolute jurisdiction of the provinces in all these matters.

Then why is the hon.
member opposing the wishes of the province of Ontario?

I beg the hon. member's pardon; I myself suggested an addition to the proposal made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on the second reading of a public bill-that it should be left to the province of Ontario, and objections came from Ontario representatives.
And voted differently.

I do not know, but many of them voted against it also. I voted against it precisely because the house refused to define and limit the scope of the bill by leaving it in the hands of the Ontario legislature to have it put into force or not. On the one hand I consider that parliament morally and constitutionally cannot force a court upon either Ontario or Quebec; and on

the other hand I do not think parliament should assume the responsibility of establishing a court of that nature without the province interested exercising its power of expression of opinion.

Has my hon. friend not on
many occasions by his silence supported the first, second and third readings of many divorce bills in the House of Commons?

As I explained to the
house the other day, I have let those bills pass on division. It was the custom to call each one and say "carried on division", and I explained to the house, and I repeat to my hon. friend, who is very fairminded and who seems to be exercised over my conscience in this matter, that I have come to the conclusion it is not the proper way to act. Because I think I have done something wrong in the past, I am endeavouring to do right in the future.
When did the hon. member become a Saul of Tarsus?

I am not speaking for
any other member; I am speaking simply for myself, and I think this method of saying "carried on division" is not sufficient; it does not carry the meaning which the hon. member for North Simcoe wants to attach to it- that we agreed to these bills. But I consider it does not sufficiently emphasize the objection we have on principle to divorce.
The only reason I have taken this attitude is to try to have the government think over the situation and come to a decision. The other day the leader of the opposition said something which is absolutely true. Even in private matters the government has the responsibility of the business of the house. The government has the responsibility of the general direction given to legislation, whether it be private or public. The proof of that is that if any piece of legislation appears to the government to be contrary to the interest of the country, or even, from a narrow point of view, to the interest of the government, it has the right and duty to appeal to the house to oppose it. That is one reason why I am trying-call it obstruction if you like; it does not matter to me-to emphasize the importance of this question. When the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the application of Mr. Phillips for the position of postmaster at Billings Bridge. On page 85 of the return to which I referred this afternoon, I find a report from the district superintendent to the postal service branch at Ottawa in regard to Mr. Phillips. It is too long to put the whole report on record, but I will read part of it. It says:
In conversation with Mr. Phillips it was ascertained that he is a garage owner at Billings Bridge and conducts a taxi service. If he were giv'en the postmastership his wife would look after the office. He stated that she had the better education, as she had been a school teacher for nine years.
Mr. Phillips was one year in England and three years in France, as a chauffeur and mechanic, but suffered no disability.
The chief superintendent then asked for information as to the order of merit of Mr. Phillips, and a further report was sent by the district superintendent to the postal service branch dated April 20, 1928. It reads:
With reference to departmental memorandum of yesterday's date, concerning an application from Mr. W. T. Phillips, for the postmastership of Billings Bridge, which was received after a report was forwarded regarding the various applicants for the postmastership, and in connection with which the district superintendent was requested to state where Mr. Phillips' name should appear in the order of merit of the applicants, it is desired to say that Mr. Phillips should precede Mr. D. T. Campbell.
In conversation with Mr. Phillips and his wife, it was ascertained that Phillips, in the event of being appointed postmaster, would continue the operation of his taxi service. It appears he has two cars on the road; the one manned by a driver during the day time, and the bulk of Phillips' work is performed after 6 o'clock. He states he would be in attendance at the office at mail hours and during the greater portion of the day, but that if post office business were slack he might absent himself. It is clearly to be seen that Mrs. Phillips would be the one who would be in constant attendance at the post office and the district superintendent was very favourably impressed with the woman's appearance and intelligence. She has been in this country fifteen years and previous to moving here was nine years a school teacher in England. Unquestionably she has the requisite qualifications to discharge the duties of the office when money order business will have been restored there.	_
As stated in the previous memorandum, it is the intention of Mr. Phillips, if he is appointed postmaster, to remove the office to the former
site, but instead of a grocery and meat business being run in conjunction with it, he would subdivide the front portion of the building where passengers for the Hunt Club could be sheltered.
That report goes to show that Phillips and his wife between them are quite capable of taking charge of the office. That report was sent to the postal service branch, Ottawa, but no action was taken to send it on to the Civil Service Commission.
Then on the 17th day of April an application was received from one Henry Lemoine. which was forwarded by the district superintendent to the postal service branch on the 25th of April. Attached to the application were recommendations from P. C. Lemoine, of Sorel, Quebec, and one by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries. No report was asked in regard to Mr. Lemoine, and no report was sent on to the Civil Service Commission.
On June 20 the chief superintendent of the post office service requested his district superintendent to ascertain what arrangements the present acting postmaster at Billings Bridge would make for the proper discharge of the money order business. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that it was in connection with the money order business that the defaulting took place. A report was made by the district superintendent on June '23rd in regard to arrangements for the money order business, and while I shall not quote the report in full, it shows that the work was very unsatisfactory, that the office was left in charge of a boy of eighteen with a limited high school education, that Mr. Campbell, the temporary appointee, was working for the International Paper Company up the Gatineau and was home only every two weeks, that while the superintendent was there he found that the mail courier desired to obtain stamps from the office and could not get them, that a patron of the office wanted a money order for nineteen dollars and the boy could not give it because they were all locked up by Campbell when he went to the market. That was the condition of the post office, and yet Campbell was retained as temporary postmaster until March 14, I think, of this year. The position had not been advertised. They did not send a report to the Civil Service Commission in order that something might be done to relieve the situation, and that is the kind of service that the people of this community were getting. Dowler was put out of office in December, 1927, on account of a shortage in his accounts and here was the work of the office being attended to in a very unsatisfactory manner.

On the 25th of June the deputy postmaster general found it necessary to communicate with the hon. member for Russell, acquainting him with the conditions and stating that it was necessary that something should be done. On July 3 the district superintendent made another full report to the postal service branch in regard to the conditions at Billings Bridge post office, reiterating what had previously been said as to the unsatisfactory conditions at that office, and yet nothing was done. But they were still open to receive applications, because I find in the file another application dated August 29 from a man named Edward Sutherland, a returned soldier. This application was received by the district superintendent and sent on to the postal service branch on September 4, but still no action was taken. It will be noted from the above that Mr. Hector Doresa mentioned is not an applicant to that office, at least in so far as the department or the district superintendent's office are aware.
The application of Hector Doresa, the man who got the appointment, had been before Mr. Coolican, the assistant deputy postmaster general, and yet he states innocently or otherwise that his application was not before him. The memorandum proceeds.
As regards the applicants who submitted their applications before the closing date of the competition-27th March-it may be stated that-

(1)	Mr. Brule is still an American citizen.
(2)	Mr. D. T. Campbell, the acting postmaster. has not proved very satisfactory sine* he took charge of the office.
(3)	Mr. John Sinclair is stated by the district superintendent not to have the necessary qualifications, whereas-
(4)	Mr. Cummings is a non-resident.
In his report covering Mr. Phillip's application the district superintendent stated that he should be placed second in the list.
What is the date of that?

October 18, 1928. It is rather interesting to note that in this same file I find an application signed by H. Doresa, dated August 3, 1929-it must mean 1928-on a form supplied by the Civil Service Commission, which is properly filled up. Hon. gentlemen will notice that Mr. Coolican's letter is dated October 18, and he says in that letter that no application was received from Mr. Doresa. It would be interesting to know where that application had been all that time.
May I call the attention of the hon. gentleman, in order to have the record correct, that the applications at that date went to the Civil Service Commission, they never came to my department at all.
How did this application go direct to them?
That was very often the case. Why attempt to make an argument out of it?

Let us follow this a little further. That application was accompanied by a petition and a report by D. F. Rowe, superintendent of employment. According to the poster notice applications were to be sent to the district superintendent. There is nothing here to show it came from the commission. I do not wish to say that the minister's statement is not correct, but there is nothing in the file to show that.
There is no need to explain it.

Then in October why did not the department, following the report to the Civil Service Commission, have the position further advertised? This was not done until some time in December. It will be remembered that they advertised first in March, 1928, and then again in December. But in the meantime the man who apparently they wanted to appoint, Mr. Doresa, had filed another application, that is, he had filed it while the advertising was going on. Then the matter was taken into

Supply-Post Office
consideration by the department and the report was made on February 12, 1929, and all the applications were sent forward, Hector Doresa, class A, standing at the top of the list. It is only fair to say of Mr. Doresa that he is a returned soldier, that he had been disabled and was in receipt of a 100 per cent pension, and that in every respect, apparently, he was well recommended. But I would point out that it was only after Doresa's application was received, all those months of delay having intervened, that the advertising was attended to. The Civil Service Commission acted on the recommendation and appointed Mr. Doresa.
It may be interesting also to note that from December, 1927, until March, 1929, the Civil Service Commission had written eleven times asking for a report in regard to this man. The letters are dated April 27, May 22, June 21, July 10, August 1-this was the first occasion on which the Assistant Deputy Postmaster General replied and said they were not yet ready to send on the report. Then there were other requests by the commission on October 4, October 30-and again the Assistant Deputy Postmaster General, by letter dated November 22, 1928, stated that they were not yet in a position to send on the report. Yet he had the report in his possession covering the four men who had applied before March 27, 1928. He had a report in regard to Mr. Phillips and in regard to Campbell. I may say that Campbell's application was accompanied by a petition signed by 218 persons served by the post office. I do not contend that Campbell as a matter of fact was entitled to the position in view of the investigation, but I say the delay was inexcusable, and it seems to me its purpose was to prevent the Civil Service Commission from functioning. Then we find the Civil Service Commission writing again on December 18, 1928, and on January 19, 1929. All applications were in at that time, yet the commission's letters were not answered. Finally on February 20, 1929, the commission sent a further request for the report and the Deputy Postmaster General sent it forward. That is the report to which I have referred.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the whole matter from beginning to end indicates that the applications that had been received were for some reason or other not suitable, but this is not disclosed in this file. The department were continually in communication with the member for the riding. He was informed of the course of events, and his advice or information was requested, and he invariably gave it. The delay in the first instance was wholly
due to a request by the member that the vacancy should not be advertised. When the department found that Campbell, who was a temporary employe, was not carrying on the office satisfactorily, and had in their hands at that time seven applications for the position, there was no excuse under the sun for withholding the report from the Civil Service Commission, and so enabling the commission to act. I submit that the action of the department savours very much of a desire on their part to act independently of the commission, and that the exercise of patronage was uppermost in the mind of the minister, who apparently was determined to act on the maxim " To the victor belong the spoils."

No, Mr. Chairman. I certainly would not consent to having it carried without replying to the hon. gentleman. If one were to believe the hon. member who has just taken his seat, one would conclude that in connection with the Billings Bridge vacancy nothing but politics was played. Now, as I have said before, there are two sides to every story. There are two sides to this case, but the hon. gentleman, although he has the full record before him, has presented only one side. The first advertisement for this vacancy was, as he stated, issued on March 27, 1927. In due time four applications were received. The inspector reported on those applications. If the hon. gentleman had read that report he would have seen why the applications were not forwarded to the Civil Service Commission. The applicants were (1) Joseph L. Brule, resident civilian, an American citizen- no need of sending bis application to the Civil Service Commission; he could not be considered under the act; (2) D. T. Campbell, resident civilian, acting postmaster, according to the qualifying officer proved unsatisfactory;
(3)	John Sinclair, resident civilian, eliminated under qualifications by investigating officer, as he was not capable of filling the position;
(4)	C. W. Cummings, non-resident civilian, and his application could not be considered under the act because he .must be a resident of the district. Everyone of the four is eliminated except D. T. Campbell, who had some post office experience, and was then acting postmaster. Under those conditions it was seen immediately that it was no use sending this report to the Civil Service Commission, and that it would be better to readvertise the vacancy. And one reason why that position was taken was that from the second day of April on-and especially on
Supply-Post Office

the 2nd day of April-the department received applications. The department received an application from W. T. Phillips. This application could not be considered because it had been received after the date fixed for the receipt of applications under the first advertisement. But having gone over the reports, and seeing that it might be necessarj' to advertise again, we held W. T. Phillips's application on file; and immediately, within a very short time after that-and Phillips is a returned soldier-there eame in another application from Edward Sutherland, a returned soldier, on August 29. That was followed by applications from other returned soldiers. The Doresa application was not received through the department, and according to the wording of the report which the hon. member read to the house on the blank form on which it was set out, it must have gone to the Civil Service Commission, who would send the application to the postal district superintendent, who in turn when the proper time came, when the second advertisement would be published, would send it in to the department, so that the inspecting officer qualified under the act might examine this applicant. That was the procedure, and all along, while it appears that there has been a good deal of delay between the first advertisement and the second, it was not due to anything political because, if it was, Campbell, so far as I know, was the man who could play the political game or call upon the Liberal party to assist him in getting this position. But Campbell was not considered at all. After that report he was eliminated; and when finally we decided, I think in December, to advertise a second time, we received a number of applications, Hector Doresa's application being in in the meantime. He was a returned soldier, a disability case.
Let me pause here to direct the attention of the committee to a very vicious personal attack made upon the Postmaster General in the London Free Press because the Postmaster General was not giving any opportunity to Doresa to be an applicant. I am blamed by the Tory press for not giving him an opportunity, and I am blamed by Tory members for having given him one, because it was politics to do so. That is the position, and I know the house will excuse the expression if I say, "You are damned if you do and you are damned if you don't." That is what happened in this case. Doresa finally got it, and the Tory press was asking for him to get it. But he did not get it from me but through the commission. This went along, and the second advertising took 
place. Doresa, a returned soldier and a disability case, was an applicant. William T. Phillips, a resident returned soldier, was an applicant. And other applicants were:
Mrs. K. Campbell, resident civilian.
Edward Sutherland, resident returned soldier.
Mrs. V. E. Dowler, resident civilian.
Jos. Henri Lemoine, resident civilian.
Jas. Henry McCullough, resident returned soldier.
John Sinclair, resident civilian.
Andrew Amos Brule, resident returned soldier.
There was the situation when the second advertisement was issued, and there are the applications we received. Upon the receipt of these applications there was no delay. There were five returned soldiers, and just as soon as it was possible to do so the report of the qualifying officer was forwarded to the Civil Service Commission. On March 16, last the commission issued a certificate in favour of Doresa and that certificate was approved of by the department over which I have the honour to preside.
Now there are the facts. The hon. member states that Doresa got the job because I wanted to play politics. I may say for the benefit of all that I got about the heaviest going over that a man ever got for the appointment of Doresa-although I was not responsible for it-from political friends who desired someone else to get the position and whose wishes were not complied with. I got a trouncing for it, and I get the same lashing to-night because this disabled returned soldier got the position.
That is the case as it stands, and I hope the house will understand that in this matter at least there was not the shadow of playing politics. No matter what I may have done in other cases, this is a case in which I can in all conscience say that there was absolutely no shadow of politics in it. I did not know a single applicant; I did not know their politics until, the appointment having been made, political friends came to me and opposed the action which, as they thought, I had taken in appointing Doresa.

How did my hon. friend
happen to make a mistake in this case?

Just like all good fellows,
one is apt to make a mistake occasionally.
I know some you made when you were Postmaster General.

is inventing mistakes I did not make.

am honest enough to admit it, but I am afraid my hon. friend will not consent to the admission on his part.

That the debate on the amendment of Mr. Stewart (Leeds), to the motion that Mr. Speaker leave the chair for the house to go again into committee of supply, be revived.
As hon. members well know, the rales of the house provide that a motion which is taken up on Wednesday on going into supply drops if that motion is not disposed of at the end of that day. When the house made that rule I think it was intended that in the event of a motion being so dropped it should not be revived. However, I have no doubt that in the present instance hon. members opposite would assume that the government had some special reason for not wishing to revive this particular motion on Monday next if it were strictly to follow the rules. And if the Postmaster General desires, as I believe he does, to have the motion revived so that it may be disposed of by vote of the house, the government will support him in that regard. I think it should be understood hereafter, however, that when an amendment is made on going into supply on Wednesday and is not disposed of, but is dropped according to the rules, the government should not be expected to permit that motion to be revived at a subsequent time.

The Prime Minister will
pardon me for interrupting him, but I think on a previous occasion last year or the year before we had a similar experience and the motion was allowed to be revived, not by the government but by the interpretation of the rules by the house.

There is another matter about which I presume the minister knows something, namely, the agitation which has been carried on for the past twenty years by certain residents of the island in the vicinity of Fort Augustus and Johnston's River, who are asking for a railway connection which I think would be better than the proposed line. There would be this added advantage which should appeal to the Canadian National officials; it would go through the territory of Johnston's River and Fort Augustus and the railway would pick up from 250 to 300 additional carloads of freight in the course of a year. The people are situated too far from the railway and they are using the river for transportation purposes. A little steamer calls once a week, but that service is very inconvenient, and they are forced to use motor boats, schooners, and every form of water transportation. its object making necessary adjustments in connection with the last three year program of branch line construction for the Canadian National Railways. And in the committee considerable inquiry was made of the officers responsible as to the reason for such heavy expense. In actual practice the work has cost even more than that provided for in the original act, I am advised that as the work was opened up, in the majority of the larger
cuttings a soft material was encountered at varying depths, from eight to eighteen feet, to ths bottom of the cuts, which in places were up to sixty feet in depth; and as the work progressed slides and slippings began to occur and continued to grow worse, in both the sloughing in of the cutting and slipping or sliding out of the embankments as the heavier parts of both the cuts and the embankments were reached. This condition has necessitated already the handling of much more material than originally figured upon, and before the work is complete it now appears that the quantities also required to be moved may be double the original figure in the estimate. speechtext:
Yes. The second item in the resolution relates to the Pilkington-Nia-gara Junction proposal of two years ago. Before this act was asked for, one of the proposals, to answer the same purpose, was to build a line from Pilkington to Montrose Junction, there join the Michigan Central railroad and obtain running rights over their line to Niagara Junction near Bridgeburg. This is the same as the present proposal by the requested amendment. At that time negotiations with the Michigan Central made it appear there was no hope of their assenting to such an arrangement.
The Pilkington-Niagara Junction line would make two crossings of the Michigan Central, the original proposals for which were protected diamonds; this, however, was objected to by the Michigan Central. An estimate was then made for grade separations of these tracks, which indicated an increased cost over the total amount voted of about one million
C .N .R .-Branch Lines

dollars. This led to further studies and interviews. The present position is that arrangements have been made with the Michigan Central that will give the Canadian National Railways joint and equal running rights over their line Montrose Junction to Niagara Junction, the terms for which are to be worked out. In order to make use of these running rights, the Canadian National would build from near Pilkington to Montrose Junction, and to effect this the present amendment of the act is being asked for, which changes the terminating point to Montrose Junction, decreases the length of the line to build about ten miles, reduces the amount voted by $414,000, and extends the time to complete by two years. This new proposal gives a route a fraction of a mile shorter and accomplishes all the purposes of the other. It requires less capital outlay, would give an opportunity to put the outskirts of Niagara Falls on this route for passenger business, and would share in the handling of the products of industries established, and that would be established, on the line Montrose to Bridge-burg. In this case there is a reduction of $414,000 in the amount asked for.

subtopic: GRAND MERE-EAST BTIRRILLS PILKINGTON-NIAGARA JUNCTION ROSEDALE SOUTHEASTERLY
speechtext:
Yes. The original intention for the joint section was for 39 miles, Rosedale to Bullpound creek. At that time the Canadian Pacific Railway intended to build easterly from near Builpound Creek as also was the intention of the Canadian National Railways, the former taking a more southerly route than the Canadian National going easterly. Since the act was passed, the Canadian Pacific Railway decided to build southerly and join their Empress-Bassano line 
at Rosemary. This necessitated their staying in the bottom of the Red Deer river valley for the last twelve miles of the original proposed joint section in order to be able to cross the river to the south, and not start to climb out of it on an easy gradient which was the first proposal and what will be the proposal of the Canadian National Railways line. This change now means that only 28.19 miles instead of 39 miles will constitute the joint section. The Canadian Pacific undertook the construction of this line, the Canadian National undertaking to pay half the cost.

In regard to the general program authorized two years ago, I might say that while these three lines show an aggregate deficiency of $229,000 as compared with the original estimate, it is only fair to the management to point out that the twenty lines authorized under the 1924-27 program were completed for $2,340,000 less than the maximum amount authorized and within $44,000 of the minimum allowed under the various acts. C.N.R.-Branch Lines
for more than, the original amount voted, with the qualification that taking all the thirty-five lines together they will be built for less than the aggregate amount voted by parliament.

less money available for construction in sections of Canada where profitable traffic may be expected. speechtext:
From the point of view of the management this never was a traffic-producing proposal ; it was advanced entirely for the purpose of reducing operating costs in connection with the present volume of traffic between Garneau Junction and Montreal, and was designed to overcome the controlling grade on that section. As my hon. friend will appreciate, I did look with some concern on the proposal when it was first put before me two years ago; it semed a large amount of money for such a small mileage of railway, but I do not remember a proposal coming to me from the management of the Canadian National Railways at any time on which the operating department, from the point of view of operating economies, were more insistent than with regard to this proposal. I am sure they will be pleased to come before the railway committee and give the reasons for the faith which is in them with respect to this particular matter. I am glad my hon. friend mentioned the viaduct, because in every case where operating economics are given as the reason for an expensive proposal of this kind I ask the management to supply me with a complete analysis of the situation; I endeavour to have them show me, so far as my understanding will permit me to go in the matter, the reasons for the faith which is in them that as a result of spending this amount, money will be saved in spite of the large capital expenditure involved. When the original proposals passed the government and were subsequently passed by the house, I have no hesitation in saying that at that time I was convinced that the cost would 'be justified by the operating economics produced in such a congested traffic district and over such a high operating grade.
My hon. friend referred to the cost of the right of way, and I think that should be inquired into when the matter comes before the railway committee. A very large area of land will have to be acquired in order to accommodate sixty-foot cuts in the class of material to which I referred a few moments ago as existing at this point. The slope will have to extend a long distance back and it will 
involve the acquisition of a considerable amount of property. It will be quite within the competence of the committee to inquire, and in fact I will see to it that the officers of the railway come to that committee prepared to give full information, as to the point of view advanced by my hon. friend. In fairness to him I must say that it is a constructive point of view, and I believe we should look at these Canadian National proposals from that angle. I agree with him that this is hardly the place to get to the bottom of it, but it is the proper place to initiate inquiries of that character. I apprehend that- his inquiry is in no sense intended as a reflection upon those who are responsible, but is rather an inquiry as to a matter which involves the voting by this parliament of a large sum of money.

subtopic: GRAND MERE-EAST BTIRRILLS PILKINGTON-NIAGARA JUNCTION ROSEDALE SOUTHEASTERLY

The main and alluring feature is the fact that we are hauling our trains from Garneau Junction to Montreal over a very high hill; our heaviest motive power can only haul less than half what the same motive power can haul upon a reasonable grade and by making this improvement we can double the amount of freight which can be hauled by one engine over the section. I cannot give my hon. friend the actual figures as to the saving, but that is a rough idea of the improvement which will be brought about. Of course, I might have answered that we are now into this thing so far that we shall have to finish it, but I do not urge that because it is a proper matter to be considered before the committee. I like the officers of the Canadian National Railways who are responsible for the spending of money-I am not speaking so much of the president as of the officers responsible for the operation and construction of the road

to feel that when they are spending money they are spending the money of the people of Canada and they must be prepared to come before a committee of the house and there state the reasons for the faith that is in them with respect to any such technical proposal. I think that is a sound principle and I am sure the officers and management of the Canadian National Railways welcome that attitude.
